p1a2: You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you've been staring at the rug. I count that as pl/ork too, even if it feels like it's in the way. Before you decide where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or what it wants, or if it just has something to say. It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or the parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.
p2c2: Sometimes it's just a thought, though, and you don't have to make a new inner person out of every sentence your mind comes up with. Go with the simplest thing that helps, like noticing "Oh, that's thinking," letting it go by, and coming back to the room you're in. Some thoughts won't go by. If one keeps coming back with a fear or a plan or a demand, maybe sounding like you at a certain age, and it all hangs together, you could try talking with it as a part of you.
p3a2: Once you have a rough idea of who's in there, naming them isn't the end of it. They react to each other too, so notice what each reaction teaches the others (I think that matters more than the names). If a part of you that's trying to protect you warns you and actually gets heard, it doesn't have to get louder. But if the inherited critic voice answers every warning with "don't be such a baby," that part learns it has to keep shouting, and your little one is right there hearing both.
p4a2: If you push past a reaction, the part of you behind it can learn that you still don't listen when it says no. You could tell it something like, "I see you. I'm not going to force my way past you. What's going on?" Or however you'd actually say that. Then wait. Don't grill the silence or fill it with a made-up answer just because you'd set this up as a healing session.
